title: The Value of Bank Durability: Borrowers as Bank Stakeholders
research_question: Do borrowing firms bear costs when their lending bank's durability is unexpectedly impaired, and do they benefit when that durability is restored? In other words, are corporate borrowers genuine stakeholders in the banks from which they borrow, such that the value of their lending relationships is reflected in their own equity values?
data_description: The sample consists of 53 publicly traded firms (listed on the NYSE or AMEX) with publicly documented lending relationships with Continental Illinois Bank during 1984. Lending relationships were identified by hand-searching the Wall Street Journal, American Banker, the Lexis database, Dow Jones News Retrieval, Standard & Poor's reports, Moody's, and corporate annual reports for 1982–1985 for tombstone advertisements and articles indicating Continental Illinois acted as direct lender, lead/colead manager of a syndicated loan, or participant lender. For 29 firms Continental Illinois was direct lender or lead manager; for 24 it was only a syndicate participant. Daily stock returns are taken from CRSP, with the equally weighted index as the market benchmark. Firm-level variables include market value of equity, total (long-term plus short-term) debt, and credit facility size, measured at year-end 1983. Mean credit facility size is $431.5 million; mean equity value is $1.085 billion.
institutional_context: The setting is the 1984 de facto failure and subsequent FDIC rescue of Continental Illinois Bank, then the seventh-largest U.S. bank holding company and a major corporate lender and syndicated-loan arranger. Beginning in March 1984 with the sale of its credit card division, the bank suffered escalating distress: discount-window borrowing, an emergency loan from 28 banks, a search for private bidders, and the Bass family's withdrawal as the last potential acquirer. On July 23, 1984, the FDIC announced it would take a controlling equity interest, effectively nationalizing the bank. This was the last episode in which the liquidation of a major U.S. money-center bank was a realistic prospect, as regulators promulgated the 'too big to fail' doctrine shortly afterward. The episode provides a setting where bank durability changed sharply for reasons external to the borrowers, allowing observation of how impaired and restored bank viability affects firms tied to the bank through different types of lending arrangements.
